meta.title: Halim Choi — ML Engineer Portfolio
meta.description: A record of collecting Korea–Japan airfare price data myself, and building and validating a forecasting model from it.

hero.keywords: Time series forecasting · Model validation · Data pipelines

about.heading: About
about.education: B.S. in Computer Software, The University of Suwon · Expected {profile.graduation|month}
about.body1: I automated daily collection of Korea–Japan airfare prices and built a price forecasting model from that data.
about.body2: I checked whether the evaluation method was right before trusting the score, and in the process corrected an inflated R² twice.
about.body3: Alongside each prediction, it also shows the range that can be trusted.

skills.collection: Collection automation — GitHub Actions collects prices daily and auto-commits the CSV
skills.modeling: Time series modeling — per-route NeuralProphet trend + XGBoost residual learning, tuned with Optuna over {model.optunaTrials} trials
skills.validation: Validation design — checked for leakage by comparing TimeSeriesSplit, GroupKFold, and K-Fold
skills.interval: Prediction interval calibration — the {model.interval.level}% interval's actual coverage is {model.interval.coverage}%

case.heading: Korea–Japan airfare: when should you buy?

problem.heading: Problem and data
problem.body1: I collected airfare prices for {data.routes} routes between Incheon and Tokyo (Narita, Haneda) and Osaka (Kansai), from {data.collectStart|date} to {data.collectEnd|date}.
problem.body2: Results come from the Google Flights search via SerpApi, run daily by GitHub Actions. Of {data.rawRows} raw rows, {data.filteredRows} remained after filtering out errors.
problem.body3: Near-term departure dates were collected daily, distant ones weekly, so the far end of the range is sparse. On the terrain, the sparse patches are that stretch.

insight.heading: Key insight
insight.body1: I tracked prices day by day for {model.realizedFlights} flights that had already departed. Right before departure ({model.bookingCurve.0.label}), prices ran {model.bookingCurve.0.pct|signed}% above the same flight's average, while the {model.bookingCurve.5.label} window was cheapest at {model.bookingCurve.5.pct|signed}%. That's a U-shaped curve about {model.curveWidth}pp wide.
insight.body2: But what moves the price more than when you buy is when you fly. Flights departing on holidays and weekends rise as peaks on the terrain.

bubble.heading: Deflating the R² bubble
bubble.body1: The first R² of {model.bubble.firstR2} I got turned out to be from the Haneda route alone.
bubble.body2: I then found and removed {data.removedImplausible} rows labeled nonstop but actually connecting flights. MAE barely changed, from ₩{model.bubble.maeBefore} to ₩{model.bubble.maeAfter}, while R² alone dropped from {model.bubble.r2Before} to {model.bubble.r2After}. Those rows made up {model.bubble.denomShare}% of the R² denominator.
bubble.body3: So I don't look at R² alone — I check it together with MAE and data integrity. Because the filter conditions differ, I don't compare this R² directly with earlier ones.

validation.heading: Validation design
validation.body1: I evaluated the same model three ways. TimeSeriesSplit, which matches production conditions, is the headline figure.
validation.body2: Evaluating on unseen departure dates with GroupKFold revealed a train/serve mismatch — on a new departure date, lookup statistics fall back to a default value. With lookup included, matching the production setup, R² was {model.gkfWithLookup.r2} and MAE was ₩{model.gkfWithLookup.mae}. I retuned and compared {model.lookupVariants} lookup configurations.

interval.heading: Prediction interval calibration
interval.body1: Instead of a single price, I also output a {model.interval.level}% prediction interval.
interval.body2: A fixed interval's actual coverage dropped to {model.interval.driftLow}% on more recent data. I adjusted the interval width to account for the shifting distribution, reaching {model.interval.coverage}% coverage on the most recent window.

limits.heading: Limitations and next steps
limits.body1: A simple baseline that just reuses the same flight's most recent observed price has an MAE of ₩{model.baselineMae}, barely different from the model's ₩{model.tss.mae}.
limits.body2: {model.reco.buyNow}% of recommendations are 'buy now.' Tracking actual prices showed that within two months of departure, waiting was on average a loss — and the model pointed the same way.
limits.body3: The next step is to beat the baseline by adding the same flight's recent observed prices as a feature.
